extracted.intended_audience: statesmen, political writers, public intellectuals interested in causes of public disorder and political rhetoric
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for diagnosing causes of public discontents and for composing persuasive, prudent political argument in essay or pamphlet form. Focuses on how to analyze popular temper, attribute causes, and recommend remedies without mistaking symptoms for systemic problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temper of the people as first study
rubrics_metrics.description: “The temper of the people amongst whom he presides ought therefore to be the first study of a statesman.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A statesman should make knowledge of popular disposition his primary inquiry; this knowledge is attainable and necessary for governing effectively. Reasoning about policy and public feeling must start from an accurate appraisal of the people's temper rather than abstract theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish general complaints from special symptoms
rubrics_metrics.description: “True political sagacity manifests itself in distinguishing that complaint which only characterizes the general infirmity of human nature, from those which are symptoms of the particular distemperature of our own air and season.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate ordinary, perennial dissatisfaction with signs of a specific political crisis. Diagnose whether discontent is merely human nature or an indication of a concrete, temporally-located malady requiring redress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption in favor of popular grievance
rubrics_metrics.description: When popular discontents are prevalent, the presumption is at least upon a par in favor of the people; it may often indicate something amiss in the constitution or government conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In disputes between rulers and subjects, give the people's complaints at least equal weight; prevalent discontent commonly implies real defects and should not be dismissed out of hand as mere folly or malice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require clear evidence before blaming libellers or factious politicians
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid explaining widespread disorder solely by 'the wicked industry of some libellers, joined to the intrigues of a few disappointed politicians' without the clearest and firmest proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skeptically evaluate claims that assign primary blame to a small group of agitators; such explanations are convenient to rulers but must be supported by solid evidence rather than rhetorical dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firmness must be paired with wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is of the utmost moment not to make mistakes in the use of strong measures; and firmness is then only a virtue when it accompanies the most perfect wisdom.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hard measures (punishment, coercion) can worsen underlying disorders if applied without deep understanding. Policy firmness is only justified when informed by sagacity and careful diagnosis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat symptoms with purely punitive remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: “Particular punishments are the cure for accidental distempers in the state; they inflame rather than allay those heats which arise from the settled mismanagement of the government.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of relying on individual punishments or prosecutions to solve systemic problems; they often inflame public anger rather than address root causes. Remedies should target institutional or policy defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid simplistic policy prescriptions (no extreme remedies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject facile solutions (e.g., introducing poverty to cure turbulence caused by wealth, or calling in despotism to fill deficiencies of law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy responses must be proportionate and realistic; do not propose extremes that are impractical or morally unacceptable as cures for political discontent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of retrospective complacency/bias
rubrics_metrics.description: “We are very uncorrupt and tolerably enlightened judges of the transactions of past ages… Few are the partisans of departed tyranny; and to be a Whig on the business of an hundred years ago, is very consistent with every advantage of present servility.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the tendency to judge past events more fairly than present ones; avoid using retrospective examples as comfortable substitutes for confronting present complexities. Historical admiration is often inconsistent with present practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for changes in political form and manners when diagnosing grievances
rubrics_metrics.description: “A great change has taken place in the affairs of this country… in the silent lapse of events as material alterations have been insensibly brought about in the policy and character of governments and nations.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume current grievances mirror those of earlier ages; analyze how institutional, cultural, and political changes alter the forms and sources of discontent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine structures of influence, intermediaries, and their transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate how influence (court influence, patronage) has operated as a substitute for prerogative and how plans to remove intermediate powers (separating court from administration, creating a 'king's men' party) alter governance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proposals and political moves by tracing how they change lines of dependence and intermediary checks (e.g., leaders, parties, Commons). Beware projects that aim to centralize power by destroying independent intermediaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze political projects by their instruments and gradual methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Study the scheme's practical steps: create a court faction, separate court from ministry, habituate Parliament to indifference to ministers' character—i.e., examine the instruments, not just the professed ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing political strategies, focus on the concrete mechanisms (party-building, disciplining representatives, replacing popular leaders) and their likely long-term effects rather than rhetorical justifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate reputational and rhetorical risks of diagnosing causes
rubrics_metrics.description: If you blame favorites of the people you will be thought a tool of power; if you censor those in power you will be looked on as an instrument of faction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors diagnosing public disorders must expect and manage attacks on their motives; weigh how naming causes may be received and craft arguments to preempt facile criticisms about partisanship or subservience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about inferring causation from timing and partial data
rubrics_metrics.description: Implied throughout (and explicitly earlier in the work): do not infer a regulation's effects from data in years when it could not yet have operated; beware using a single year's figures to prove causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure chronological plausibility and adequate evidence before attributing causes to policy changes. Check whether a measure could realistically have produced observed effects in the claimed timeframe and use sustained trends rather than isolated observations.
